thread.title: What Type Of Stock Is Starbucks? - Starbucks Corporation (NASDAQ:SBUX)

author: SA Editor Daniel Shvartsman
title: What Type Of Stock Is Starbucks? - Starbucks Corporation (NASDAQ:SBUX)
text:
Every type of stock market investment has, I hope it's safe to assume, the same general goal - to return more money than is originally invested. Each investment comes with its own risk and its own potential reward, and hopefully the rewards outweigh the risks over the long term in each case. How an investor achieves the return may differ - one might be looking for income rather than capital gains, while another is taking a series of risky bets hoping for one big payout that makes up for the others, and so on. But the end zone looks the same.
What might suit my style of investing might not suit yours, which is one of the many things that make a stock market interesting. We can both be right about the same company while holding differing views, based on our investment approach. I might think that a stock is going to do poorly in the next two years and you may think it will be a winner over the next five, for example. Happens all the time.
Starbucks ( SBUX ) has been a great American success story for decades. Per yCharts, since coming public in the 90s, the company has had a total return of ~17000%. The company's coffee shops are ubiquitous, found on corners and in airports and malls around the world. It has expanded to different categories, and generally maintained a decent corporate reputation.
For this edition of Editor's Notes - a series where I review articles published on Seeking Alpha and highlight common themes and takeaways - I reviewed the recent conversation around Starbucks to see what our authors are saying about the company, and how they are viewing its fit (or lack thereof) in their portfolios.
A Quick Review Of The Fundamentals Over the past three years, the Starbucks stock story has changed, at least. The shares have had a negative total return, as compared to strong numbers from the S&P 500 ( SPY ) and the Consumer Discretionary Sector (represented by XLY )
SBUX Total Return Price data by YCharts
Recently, the company has lowered its guidance ; announced the departure of long-time Executive Chairman Howard Schultz, the man most associated with Starbucks; and has taken a reputation hit for the issue in Philadelphia where a store manager called the police on two men waiting in the shop. It would seem news is following along with the stock price, causing that dip you see at the end of the chart above.
I'm not a Starbucks fan, per se - I'm more of a tea drinker, which is best made at home - but the company seems pretty well entrenched in our modern global society. It's not exactly McDonald's ( MCD ) opening its first store in post-Soviet Russia and getting lines stretching down the streets in the hundreds, but it's a company that isn't likely to go anywhere in the next 10 years. The balance sheet is fairly healthy, the company is generating a good amount of free cash flow, and revenue and earnings are growing.
So the question this brings me to is 'what type of investment is Starbucks, and how can we tell?'
Reviewing the numbers SBUX Revenue (NYSE: TTM ) data by YCharts
Source: 2017 10K
To start, the company is still valued at a healthy multiple. I get just above 25x price to trailing twelve months free cash flow, and the company has net debt, so the enterprise value multiple is higher.
I included a chart of their comparable sales. Starbucks does a really nice job disclosing those numbers, and it makes it easier to track things. We can see that consolidated comparable store sales growth has slowed from the 5-7% range to 3% in FY 2017. This has further gone down to 2% in 2018 so far (the company has reported two of its four quarters for fiscal year 2018). This is discouraging given the company set out to accelerate U.S. comparable store sales as a key operational priority in its 10K.
The other area that you would expect growth, then, would be in new stores. A big part of the growth story is China, and we'll get to that below. But the recent update that included lowered 2018 guidance also mentioned fewer net stores were going to be opened. So whatever part of the growth story that is, it's smaller than it was previously.
What's nice about Starbucks is you can probably model out the growth of the company - assuming 3-5% as your baseline growth rate, add in whatever growth you expect from new stores, and whatever operating margin improvement you deem reasonable. Is 10% net income growth doable? 15%? What surprises would Starbucks have to generate more growth? Their Q4 transcript guidance calls for: "Comp growth of 3% to 5%, revenue growth in the high single digits, and EPS growth of 12% or better....but we believe that these new targets represent performance that we can meet or beat in the years ahead."
Is that worth paying 25x trailing free cash flow for? If not, what is there in Starbucks shares to get excited about?
I'm going to break this down by looking at four different themes that come up most often in our Starbucks coverage, and see what the coverage says about Starbucks at $50/share. The four themes:
China Dividend Leverage Valuation China - If You're Looking For Growth, Where Else? If there is a growth story, it has to rest upon China. Dining Stocks Online , for example, wrote the article " With 4 Locations At 1 Seattle Shopping Center, Starbucks Should Close Far More Than 150 Stores ." The author's point is clear, and while commenters push back on a couple salient points - a, that Starbucks is underrepresented in less dense areas, and b, that licensed locations in other stores isn't as big a deal - it is hard to imagine there is that much white space left for Starbucks, or blue space if you use Starbucks's recent presentation (slide 16).
Billy Duberstein writes that Starbucks: Still A Dividend Growth Investor's Dream After Schultz's Retirement . His case starts with Schultz's main legacy - the company's culture of investing in the long term. But it focuses on China, pointing out how the company has expanded store count in China from under 500 to 3300 from 2012-2018. The continued opportunity to expand in that market and to grow coffee consumption habits among the Chinese people appear to support a higher multiple and continued growth.
Detroit Bear , another strong author, says that Stuck In Neutral: Starbucks Is A Buy On APAC Growth . They address one of the concerns I have with the China story - that comparable store sale growth is only 3% year over year - by citing the accelerating growth of stores. But more to the point, there's this paragraph that seems to be the center of the China discussion:
The story here is not about a quarter of comps or results, however. It is about the long-term potential growth of the market. Remember, Starbucks is selling an addictive product in a country that has an annual coffee consumption rate of half a cup per year relative to US consumption of 300 cups per year. The middle class in China that could purchase cups of Starbucks will be about double the population of the entire US.
On the other side of the trade, there comes the question from The Basis Point , Is Starbucks Ex Growth? They tackle the China point by changing the question a little, in reference to all the growth bulls expect in China:
But, of course, this is not the way to look at it at all. China is not as rich as America. Currently, each store in the U.S. is supported by $1.33bn of GDP while each store in China is supported by $3.61bn. If Starbucks had the same number of stores per unit of GDP in China as the company has today in the U.S., it would have 8,400 stores. Given that today Starbucks has about 3,100 stores in China, this straight GDP comparison suggests that the market for Starbucks could grow to be 2.7 times its current size. Bigger, certainly, but not wildly so.
And then, we need to consider price differentials. According to Market Watch, in May 2017, Starbucks was charging $7.18 for a grande latte in China - a drink that retails for $2.75 in the U.S. Starbucks is a much more expensive luxury in China than it is in the U.S. How many folks in China can afford to pay $7 for a cup of coffee? According to McKinsey and The Basis Point estimates, about 45m Chinese people earned more than $34,000 (the very least, we would think, anyone would need to earn to be paying $7 for a beverage) in 2015, a number which is estimated to grow to about 67m by 2022.
If the growth opportunity is capped by the lower GDP, the pricing on the coffee, and the tastes of the Chinese consumer, it's not a no-brainer support for the 20+ multiple that Starbucks sports. Keep in mind too, that China is 20% of revenue currently, so if it's not growing fast, it is not going to have much impact on Starbucks's overall growth trajectory.
Michael Boyd has been the most vocal SBUX bear in 2018, and had two China oriented pieces:
Starbucks: Heightened Leverage, All-In Bet On China Tastes Sour
Starbucks: Capital Allocation In Question
I like a couple things about the analysis here. In the first piece, he provides more context on the China opportunity:
There is no doubt that Chinese consumers are taking to the company's products, but the Chinese business still represents <15% of likely fiscal 2018 operating income even after the East China balance sheet consolidation. It's a needle mover, but only incrementally over the short to medium term. It's incredibly difficult, in my view, to think about where China will be economically five years from now. Five years ago, Xi Jinping had not yet taken office and laid out his "China Dream" policy to begin working through the state's corruption problems. No one at the time was looking for him to tighten his grip on forcing Chinese industry direction or that he would eventually consolidate power to the point of taking life-long control over the world's most populous country.
The second features some on-the-ground observations, though those are tough to extrapolate from. More interesting to me is his point about the underlying tell in Starbucks's decision to maintain a share buyback program (one that they have subsequently ramped up):
I have just one question for Starbucks bulls: If the pipeline for new Chinese store openings is so great, and rates of return are so strong, why on earth is management so intent on plowing capital into share buybacks with such low rates of return by comparison?
The articles also highlight leverage concerns for Starbucks, which makes a convenient segue to the next topic.
Leverage - Corporate Shuffling Of The Deck, Or Meaningful? Starbucks has increased its targeted total shareholder return from $15B to $25B over the next three fiscal years, which means the dividend will grow (it was just raised), but also that a lot of money is getting spent on buying back shares.
On the one hand, this puts a regular bid on the stock, which would seem to support the share price technically. On the other hand, this money comes from somewhere.
Starbucks: Buy This Dip by Global Dividends focuses on the leverage issue and argues that this is fine. Leverage will still be around 3x EBITDA, the company has a stable and growing business, free cash flow yield is much higher than the likely interest rates the company will have to pay on their debt - 7.9% vs. 2.5-3%. So buying back shares enables the company to capture a spread on the market.
This seems reasonable, and the implicit point is that even with the Fed raising interest rates regularly, they are still relatively low. Perhaps now is the best time to lock in lower interest rates to capture this corporate finance arbitrage?
On the other side, Stone Fox Capital argues that this is just $25 Billion To Nowhere . The main quote to our overall theme: "The key investor takeaway is that the growth phase is over for Starbucks and the transition of (Schultz) out of the company should cause investors to pause."
And one last point on the leverage is something Boyd raises in his first article, namely that operating leases are going to come on the balance sheet soon due to accounting rules. It looks like Starbucks is already accounting for this in their presentations, but it may not be reflected in their ratios. Between that and a loss of EBITDA due to a deal with Nestle ( OTCPK:NSRGY ), the company's leverage ratios may get close to 3 without even adding new debt.
So the questions about growth have been raised. As have questions about how sustainable the capital return is, or what that means for the business. So that brings us to the third pillar of the investment discussion.
Dividend - is Starbucks's dividend growth independent from the rest of the growth story? Most authors who cover the dividend as a focal point are bullish about it. So I'll share their views and then play devil's advocate on a few points.
Starbucks: 2.7% Yield And 20% Dividend Growth by Nicholas Ward pulls together a few themes. First, he highlights the transition of Starbucks from growth to value, which means, "that it will take time a bit of time for the market to smooth out the valuation wrinkles." He then points out that the dividend just saw a 20% increase, and that the company usually bottoms out at 20x trailing twelve month earnings. A nearly 3% yield and regular dividend growth may make the transition to value multiples less painful.
Discount Fountain is also explicit about how they view Starbucks, saying, " Starbucks: Not Holding For Growth, But For Dividends ." They highlight that the company has grown the dividend 50% over the past 3 years while still having a payout ratio of under 50%, and that is all while free cash flow has not grown. If free cash flow grows 10% a year, the dividend will have a lot of room to keep growing. But of course, that's a big question - will free cash flow growth achieve that sort of level?
Starbucks: A 2035 Dividend Aristocrat by No Guilt also plays up the dividend angle, arguing that the company will continue raising the dividend for the next 17 years. Which, sure, of course that would be good. There are some quirky arguments that slip in to support the qualitative case that Starbucks will be able to grow the dividend:
America's cultural cache will support the company's international growth as people associate Starbucks with America. I'd love to see some data on this - as an American abroad, I can buy that some U.S. brands have this cache, or that American styles and foods are popular internationally, but it's not obvious to me that Starbucks is at the top of this list. Starbucks could become the next place to meet dates: "In the age of tinder/online dating, you could have a cheap coffee date for $6 instead of a $100+ dinner. Starbucks is rapidly becoming the world's "coffee bar"." Plausible, but not sure I'd invest on that. Relative valuation, which is one of my least favorite arguments. Coca Cola ( KO ) is overvalued and WeWork ( VWORK ) is very overvalued - doesn't mean Starbucks is undervalued. But the qualitative arguments are interesting, and I think they make an underlying point - even if Starbucks is a dividend or dividend growth stock, it has to continue to grow its business well to be able to support that. 5% EPS and dividend growth over the long-term is less interesting than 10%, for example.
And if we're truly calling Starbucks a value stock, what does that mean for its multiple? Well...
Valuation - How Are We Defining A Value Stock At the beginning of the year, Robert Reisen argued that Starbucks is The Best-Valued Fast Food Stock . He stacked the company up against peers ranging from Chipotle ( CMG ) to McDonald's to Domino's ( DPZ ) and found it cheaper on an EV/FCF, Price/Sales, and Price to Earnings Growth ratio. Which is good, but 31x EV/FCF is still a high number, and the input for long-term earnings growth was 13.6%, which is no small hurdle.
The stock has pulled back some since that article was shared, but it still leaves the question of 'what is the right multiple for Starbucks?' And I think this was really well answered in Cory Cramer's piece, Starbucks Valuation: When To Catch This Falling Knife .
Cramer does a good job in his work of analyzing companies in a cyclical context. In this case, he compares Starbucks's current period to Apple ( AAPL ) in the middle of the 2010s and McDonald's around the same time, as well as during the dot com bubble. He then looks at how the stock has pulled back historically (as much as 78% in 2007-09), and the transition to a fully post-Howard Schultz world for SBUX. The analysis on CEO Kevin Johnson's recent interview on CNBC is quite cutting.
What I like about this analysis is the idea of pattern matching to find a way into the story, and to try to answer the multiple question. Cramer ends up with a basic 15x PE multiple. Put that on TTM or projected 2018 earnings, and the initial entry range becomes $32-42.
This seems to suit what a value multiple might be. I can quibble and say 15x is really the entry multiple for a GARP company, but if we give credit to the company's growing dividend, the overall quality of Starbucks over time, and some potential for growth abroad, this seems fairer than hoping it might fall to 10x.
I also like this analysis because Cramer says, "I've never been in a Starbucks store." I don't drink coffee much and avoid chain stores, but that's real dedication to never enter one.
Pouring down the last brew So what type of stock is Starbucks right now?
It's still trading like a GARP to Growth stock. 20x 2018 non-GAAP earnings, with most of the growth in earnings coming from tax reform, is a healthy multiple, and the balance sheet and free cash flow metrics make the valuation higher still. The fact that it has had a pullback doesn't mean it's fallen out of that range yet.
The broader market context is still one of healthy multiples - the Coca Cola reference is helpful on that front. In that context, you could do worse than Starbucks. I also don't think there's a literal procession where growth investors sell to GARP investors who sell to dividend growth investors who sell to value investors, so I don't know what might happen with the share price over coming months.
But the company seems to be settling in to steady returns. They've decided that the major investment they can make is in their own shares, despite the 20x multiple. That concerns me for its future prospects. It's one thing for Apple to print money with iPhones and play around with their huge cash load to buy back a lot of shares and raise dividends. In Starbucks' case, the cash cow story isn't quite strong enough to be buyable.
The dividend will probably grow over time, and is just below 3% yield at this point. The growth story in China does not seem likely enough to support the multiple, so I'm not sure what investors will see for capital gains. Add those factors up, and the investment case does not look super promising to me.
What type of stock is Starbucks? I think it's a low-return, avoid stock at current multiples. It's not so much that uncertainty is the issue, it's that the path seems fairly certain and the price too high for that path.
But that's my takeaway from reviewing our coverage and recent events. What do you think? Let me know, I'd love to hear what I'm missing.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
